The eight networks defined would fulfill this requirement for the business, giving eight

network is 256 (2^8, given that eight bits in the last octet are reserved for host IPs in a Class C
configuration).
This may not be an issue when using private IP address ranges, but applying the same
approach to the limited number of public IP addresses creates a lot of wastage. Furthermore,
most internet service providers (ISPs) and cloud providers charge a fee for public IP addresses.
To illustrate how subnetting works, consider a network built with the IP address range of
192.168.1.0 and a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0. The following diagram in Figure 7.13
illustrates this class C network and its binary representation.
Figure 7.12: IP Address Class C Network
This network has 256 IP addresses and can host 254 devices. However, the business requires
eight subnetworks, each with a idx_f5194b22 capacity to host up to 30 devices. The IP address range
192.168.1.0 can be further divided into subnetworks by borrowing bits from the fourth octet
(the host portion) to represent the subnetworks that fall within the original Class C network.

Recall that you can only host 254 devices, even though there are 256 IP addresses in
total in a Class C network, because the first and last IP addresses cannot be used. The
first IP address of any network is the network ID, and the last IP address is reserved for
broadcast traffic.

If you were to borrow just three bits from the far left of the fourth octet (the host portion), you
could create eight subnetworks within the 192.168.1.0 larger network. The following formula
derives this:
Number of subnets = 2 ^ (number of host bits borrowed)
In this example, 2^3 = 8, giving you eight subnetworks as the business requires. By borrowing 3
bits, you now have 5 bits left to represent the host portion. This will define the total number of
IP addresses available in each subnetwork. This number can be calculated using the formula:
Number of IP addresses per subnetwork = 2 ^ (Number of host bits remaining)
In this example, 2^5 = 32, each of the eight subnetworks can have a maximum of 32 IP
addresses. Remember that for every network, you have one IP address reserved for the network
ID and one IP address for the broadcast IP. Thus, the total number of usable IP addresses for
host devices is 30 (32 - 2).
Note that when borrowing bits from the host portion of the IP range, you have a different
subnet mask than the original network. This is illustrated in Figure 7.13:
Figure 7.13: Subnet mask of new subnetworks created

bits to represent the network, you create eight subnetworks within the more extensive Class C
network, which has a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0.

Using a subnet mask, you can define multiple networks and subnet networks. However, the
process is cumbersome as per the discussion so far. Another method of determining network
sizes and the number of IPs hosted idx_dada9f44 per network is to use a CIDR (Classless Interdomain
Routing) notation. This is discussed in the next section.
Classless Inter-Domain routing
Using CIDR notations, you can easily idx_87b87fac define networks of different sizes just as you use subnet
masks. Network devices convert the CIDR notation into the subnet mask for your subnet. CIDR
notations use a suffix (/n) to indicate the idx_691d3df4 number of bits used for the network portion of an IP
address. So, for example, 192.168.1.0/24 means that you are using 24 bits out of the 32-bit
range to represent the network. This is the same as using the first three octets or a subnet mask
of 255.255.255.0, which is a Class C network.
Furthermore, given that /24 indicates the number of network bits, the remaining 8 bits (32 -
24) define the total number of IP addresses you can have in that network. This is calculated as 2
^ 8, which equals 256. Remember that a network's first and last IP addresses are reserved for
network ID and broadcast; you have 254 usable IP addresses.
Most modern devices allow you to define networks and IP ranges using this CIDR notation,
which is much easier to handle. Furthermore, you can easily define variable-length subnet
masks with CIDR. So, in the earlier example of the IP address 192.168.1.0 with a subnet mask
of 255.255.255.224, you are borrowing 3 bits from the fourth octet. The CIDR notation for the
same network would be 192.168.1.0/27 (24 bits from the first three octets plus three bits
borrowed from the fourth) for the subnetworks. Working out the number of subnetworks is
181 AWS Networking Services, Part 1 – Virtual Private Cloud (VPCs)
calculated by taking 2^3, which equals eight subnetworks. Finally, you have 5 bits remaining,
giving you a total of 32 (2^5) IP addresses or 30 usable IP addresses.
The following diagram in Figure 7.17 illustrates standard CIDR blocks and their equivalent
subnet mask representations:
Figure 7.16: Standard CIDR notation and equivalent subnet masks
CIDR notations and subnet masks both define network boundaries, but CIDR is more than just
an alternative notation for subnet idx_c8c5dd14 masks. CIDR is a broader concept that includes both
subnetting and route aggregation, which is also known as supernetting. CIDR allows ISPs to
summarize idx_79ece603 multiple networks into one route, reducing the size of idx_ee1592cc global routing tables. For

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio

example, instead of advertising 192.168.0.0/24, 192.168.1.0/24, and 192.168.2.0/24, an
ISP can summarize them as 192.168.0.0/22.
Now that you have learned about the fundamentals of networks, IP addressing, subnet masks,
and CIDRs, it's time to look at how to design and build virtual networks in the cloud. Many
AWS services require you to provide them within isolated networks you define, enabling you to
apply firewall rules to dictate what type of traffic is allowed into those networks. This is where
the AWS Virtual Private Cloud (VPCs) come in, and is the topic of the next section.
Building virtual networks with Amazon VPC
A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is a virtual idx_f4665f23 network within your AWS account that enables you
idx_a03b84b5 to isolate and manage workloads idx_785912c9 efficiently. You can create multiple VPCs, each dedicated to a
specific application stack. For instance, one VPC could host a customer loyalty application,
including all necessary resources such as compute, storage, networking, and databases, while
another VPC supports an internal business intelligence tool. This segmentation enhances
security and ensures compliance by isolating workloads.
When you create a VPC, it idx_b303c9fd spans the entire AWS region where it is deployed. This allows
resources within the VPC to be distributed across multiple availability zones using the subnets

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio

you define. Since subnets operate at the availability zone level, you can idx_a2ebeb80 deploy redundant
application components across zones to ensure high availability. As shown in Figure 7.17,
resources within a VPC can communicate seamlessly over AWS's high-speed network, even if
they physically reside in different subnets that belong to that VPC. This is possible because all
subnets within a VPC share the same IP address CIDR block.
Figure 7.17: VPCs span entire regions, and subnets span specific availability zones
These subnets are logically part of the same VPC but are physically hosted on hardware located
in different data centers across multiple availability zones. The ability to create such logical
networks over distances, enabled by high-speed links and network connectivity, ensures
redundancy in the event of an availability zone failure.
For example, suppose you host a replica of your application across these subnets, and the
availability zone eu ‑ west ‑ 2a experiences an idx_0ef84030 outage. In that case, customers can still access the
application servers running in idx_26c47b1c the other two subnets, which are physically located in the
remaining availability zones.
Subnets can be either private or public. Public subnets allow you to host resources that can be
assigned public IP addresses and made directly accessible from the Internet. These typically
include resources you want to expose publicly, such as a management server for remote access
or a load balancer. In contrast, private subnets restrict direct inbound Internet access.
However, resources in a private subnet can still idx_ba560bf6 access the Internet through a Network
Address Translation (NAT) service, which is discussed in detail in a later section.
The following section provides a detailed explanation of how to configure your VPC for
Internet access.

Internet access
VPCs can be configured with Internet access, allowing you to publish applications and make
them accessible to end users or customers idx_89e2f4f1 on the Internet. To enable Internet access for your
VPC, you must deploy idx_c52d6da8 an Internet Gateway (IGW)—a highly idx_f434b4fc available, AWS-managed
service. Additionally, you need to configure the route tables to ensure that traffic from the VPC
destined for the Internet is directed to the Internet Gateway.
As depicted in Figure 7.18 and discussed earlier, a VPC idx_46c0915e can be configured with public subnets
with a direct route to the Internet Gateway via an associated route table. You will note that the
route table has a route to the Internet referenced as the IP CIDR 0.0.0.0/0; its target is the
Internet Gateway (IGW). This idx_6737089e configuration allows resources idx_110817cf within these subnets to connect

to the Internet. However, these resources idx_ed0ecbb6 must be assigned a public IP address or an Elastic IP
(EIP).
Figure 7.18: Enable internet access for VPCs
An Elastic IP (EIP) is a static, public IPv4 idx_3220a824 address you can allocate and associate with an
instance in your VPC. Unlike a standard public IP, which changes if the instance is stopped and
restarted, an EIP remains constant until you manually release it. This makes EIPs useful for
applications that require a fixed public IP address, such as hosting services or failover
scenarios. However, AWS charges for EIPs, so it's best to release any that are not actively used.

The Internet Gateway acts as a bridge, allowing idx_a265e073 resources with public IPs to send and receive
traffic directly from the Internet. The gateway enables responses to reach the intended
resource by maintaining the mapping between its public and private IP addresses.
In addition to resources in public subnets, you idx_268fb2bc may have resources in private subnets that also
need Internet access—for example, to download software updates or critical patches. These
resources do not have a public IP since they must remain private while still being able to reach
the Internet. This setup is similar to how a typical home network works: devices like laptops
and desktops do not have public IP addresses but can still access the Internet via a home router
or modem. This capability is made idx_599cf227 possible through a service known as Network Address
Translation (NAT), which is the focus of the next section.
Network address translation (NAT)
At the beginning of this chapter, you discovered how corporate networks are divided into
smaller subnetworks. In AWS, when idx_052e6e93 you build VPCs, you deploy certain specific resources in
public subnets, also idx_bb23be7e known as the DMZ, while others are placed in private subnets for
security. By deploying resources in a private subnet, you ensure they are not idx_6956ddac directly accessible
from the Internet. These resources include database servers and application servers, which
should only be accessible through frontend web servers or load balancers. This setup ensures
that any traffic to backend services is proxied through frontend web servers, preventing direct
exposure to the Internet.
However, some application servers in private subnets still require Internet access, for example,
to download software updates, security patches, or product updates. Since these servers do not
have public IP addresses, you need a mechanism idx_55b7f713 to allow outbound Internet access. This is
where Network Address Translation (NAT) comes in.
As illustrated in Figure 7.19, the NAT service acts as an intermediary, allowing resources in
private subnets to access the Internet without being directly exposed. AWS provides the NAT
Gateway, which must be deployed in a public subnet and assigned an Elastic IP address.
Outbound traffic from private subnet resources is forwarded to the NAT Gateway, which then
routes the traffic to the idx_69b99e94 Internet.
185 AWS Networking Services, Part 1 – Virtual Private Cloud (VPCs)
Figure 7.19: Internet access for resources in private subnets via NAT gateway
To enable this process, you must configure the route table for the private subnets to direct
Internet-bound traffic to the NAT Gateway instead of the Internet Gateway. The NAT Gateway
performs a one-to-many mapping, translating requests from multiple instances' private IP

addresses to its public IP address before forwarding them to the Internet. When responses are
received, the NAT Gateway relays them back to the original requesting instance in the private
subnet.
While Internet Gateways and NAT Gateways enable you to provide Internet access to resources
in your VPC, you must also consider what type of traffic you allow inbound and outbound from
your VPC. Restricting idx_19bfcf1e traffic to only what is required for your application's specific use case is
critical in preventing malicious attacks. VPC security is discussed in the next section.
Securing VPC traffic
When configuring your VPC, AWS provides multiple security features to control the flow of
traffic into, out of, and within your idx_12313e65 cloud network. These features help ensure that only
authorized traffic reaches your applications and resources.
For instance, you may allow inbound traffic to your web servers from the internet on port 80
(HTTP) and/or port 443 (HTTPS). HTTPS ensures encrypted connections to your web servers.

Once a request reaches the web server, it may need to communicate with a backend MySQL
database to store and retrieve data. You can allow traffic from the web servers to the database
on port 3306 (MySQL's default port) to enable this. By restricting access to only approved
sources—such as the web servers—you prevent unauthorized resources inside and outside the
VPC from connecting directly to the database.
AWS provides two key firewall services to help secure your VPC: Security Groups and
Network Access Control Lists (NACLs), discussed in the following subsections.
Security groups
Security Groups act as virtual firewalls that control inbound and outbound traffic at the
resource level. They are primarily idx_99ab8d5b used with resources such as EC2 instances, Lambda
functions, ECS containers, and RDS database instances, all requiring a network interface to
communicate within a VPC, other networks, or the internet.
As shown in Figure 7.20, a Security Group is associated with a resource's network interface,
allowing you to specify which traffic (ports and protocols) is permitted for both inbound and
outbound communication. Since every resource has at least one primary network interface,
you must attach one Security Group to define the allowed traffic flows.
Figure 7.20: Security group associated with EC2 instance
The diagram showcases an inbound idx_95221ebe rule that allows traffic on port 80 (HTTP) from the
Internet. This would allow users on the Internet to access your website hosted on this server.
You can have up to five security groups associated with an instance.
187 AWS Networking Services, Part 1 – Virtual Private Cloud (VPCs)
Each VPC has a default Security Group that allows inbound connectivity from itself on all
protocols and ports. This is a default setting that ensures multiple resources, such as EC2
instances attached to the default group, can communicate with each other on any port.
Security Groups act as stateful firewalls, meaning that if you define an outbound rule to allow
access to the internet on ports 80 and 443, the responses to those requests will automatically
be allowed inbound. Conversely, suppose you define an inbound rule to allow users from the
internet to access a web server on port 80, as shown in Figure 7.20. In that case, the
corresponding outbound responses are automatically permitted.
Security Groups operate idx_70f2bbdf on a deny-by-default principle, meaning you must define inbound
rules before any traffic can reach the resources attached to the Security Group. Additionally,
explicit deny rules cannot be configured.
For example, if you allow inbound idx_14a21fcc traffic from the entire internet (0.0.0.0/0) on a specific
port, you cannot then deny inbound traffic on port 80 from a specific IP address range. If you

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio

need to block traffic from a particular source explicitly, you must use NACLs, which are
discussed in the next section.
Network access control lists (NACLs)
Network Access Control Lists (NACLs) act as firewalls at the subnet level, allowing you to
define exactly what traffic is permitted into and idx_02f57601 out of a subnet. Within the subnet, resources
have Security Groups attached to them for additional traffic restrictions at the resource level.
NACLs are often considered a secondary firewall solution, providing an additional layer of
security alongside Security Groups. By default, AWS creates a default NACL that allows all
inbound and outbound traffic. However, organizations typically create custom NACLs that
deny all traffic by default and then explicitly define which ports and protocols are allowed
inbound and outbound.
NACLs are particularly useful when different types of resources exist within a subnet, ensuring
only permitted traffic flows in and out.
Unlike Security Groups, NACLs support explicit deny rules. This is possible due to the way
NACLs process traffic:
Inbound and outbound rules are evaluated in order, based on rule numbers (lower
numbers have higher priority)
As shown in Figure 7.21, an inbound rule numbered 50 denies traffic from a specific IP
CIDR block (192.168.5.0/24) on port 443

You will also notice a catch-all entry with the rule numbered as a wildcard (*). This rule denies

A key feature of Network Access Control Lists (NACLs) is that they are stateless. Unlike
Security Groups, which automatically allow return traffic, NACLs require explicit inbound
and outbound rules for bidirectional traffic flow. If you allow inbound traffic, you must also
define a corresponding outbound rule to permit the response traffic.
You can create multiple VPCs in your AWS account across all regions. Sometimes, you may
wish to have resources in these VPCs communicate with each other. While this can be done via
the Internet Gateway, you should also ensure that communications between VPCs do not
traverse the public Internet. This can be achieved by idx_638c8f48 using a feature known as VPC Peering,
which is idx_c8ac6d86 the topic of the next section.
Connecting VPCs with VPC peering
A VPC peering connection is a private network link between two VPCs, allowing resources in
one VPC to access those in another. Peering idx_a60256ef connections can be within the same region or
across regions, enabling organizations to build global-scale network architectures. This is
especially useful for data sharing across regions, whether for disaster recovery (DR) purposes
or to idx_c3407eb2 bring resources closer to end customers in a distributed setup.
•
•
189 AWS Networking Services, Part 1 – Virtual Private Cloud (VPCs)
While AWS manages the underlying infrastructure to ensure high availability and fault
tolerance, users must manually configure peering connections, update route tables, and adjust
NACLs and Security Groups to allow traffic between the connected VPCs.
However, standard VPC peering has limitations. Each peering connection must be explicitly
defined, meaning that if multiple VPCs need to communicate, each connection must be set up
individually. As per the diagram in Figure 7.22, transitive routing is not supported, preventing
traffic from automatically flowing between peered VPCs.
Figure 7.22: VPC peering configuration
In Figure 7.22, you can see that there is an explicit peering connection between VPC A and VPC
B, as well as between VPC A and VPC C. However, it is important to note that even though VPC
A is connected to both VPC B and idx_e17900cd VPC C, resources in VPC B cannot communicate with
resources in VPC C unless there is a direct peering connection between them.

This requirement to define explicit peering connections can soon become very complex and
add administrative overhead. As discussed in the next section, AWS offers another service to
help address this.
Centralizing VPC connectivity with AWS Transit
Gateway
AWS VPC Transit Gateway is designed to help connect multiple VPCs both within and across
regions through a standard hub-and-spoke idx_1b767420 model. As depicted in Figure 7.23, this simplifies
the network architecture as new VPCs peered to the gateway need just a single connection to

route traffic to other VPCs in the configuration. Unlike VPC Peering, which requires direct
connections between VPCs, Transit Gateway provides a high-performance, scalable
interconnect with optimized routing.
Figure 7.23: VPC transit gateway
Your VPC Transit Gateway can also be used to connect to an on-premises network, enabling
you to easily access all other VPCs through it.
As well as enabling connectivity idx_f2b18f73 between VPCs, you may wish to connect to your VPC from on-
premises locations and data centers. You must secure this connection, and this is where you
can configure Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), which is discussed in the next section.
Securing hybrid connectivity with VPNs
Many companies need to idx_ef86771a securely connect to their AWS-hosted VPCs to carry out various
tasks. While connecting over the Internet is an option, organizations often prefer a more secure
connection, especially for backend operations. You can configure a Virtual Private Network
(VPN) connection idx_10a5326e to facilitate this. This connection traverses the public Internet but secures
data using AES-128 or AES-256-bit Internet Protocol Security (IPSec) encryption, ensuring
191 AWS Networking Services, Part 1 – Virtual Private Cloud (VPCs)
that data transfers remain unreadable by idx_f28eadc5 unauthorized parties. Often referred to as
establishing a secure VPN tunnel, this approach enhances overall security.
As depicted in Figure 7.24, you can set up a site-to-site VPN connection by configuring a VPN
Gateway and attaching it to your VPC. Additionally, you must deploy a customer gateway, a
hardware or software service located on the on-premises network that connects to the VPG
over the Internet. Once the VPN connection is established, you must configure the necessary
route table to ensure traffic is properly routed across the VPN connection.
Figure 7.24: IPSec site-to-site VPN tunnel
IPSec VPN tunnels are designed to encrypt the traffic between the VPC and your on-premises
data center. However, the bandwidth would be limited by your Internet connection from your
on-premises location. Further, there idx_a05ba94d is a hard limit set by AWS, which caps at 1.25 Gbps per
tunnel. You can use the AWS Direct Connect service discussed in the next section if you require
more bandwidth and a dedicated connection that bypasses the public Internet.

Connecting on-premises networks with AWS Direct
Connect
Direct Connect is a service that enables you to connect your corporate data center to your VPC
and other public services offered by AWS over a dedicated fiber optic network connection. This
network connection is completely idx_091635f2 private and does not traverse the public Internet.
This solution is more expensive but helps address higher bandwidth requirements. With Direct
Connect, you can configure dedicated connections offering speeds of 1, 10, or 100 Gbps.
While understanding the fundamentals of VPCs is essential, getting hands-on experience will
help you build much-needed practical skills. The following section covers creating a VPC in

The following section provides a summary of this chapter.
Summary
AWS Virtual Private Cloud is a service that enables you to build secure, isolated networks in
your AWS account to host your application workloads. This allows you to separate workloads
for various reasons, including compliance and security. A VPC spans an entire AWS region,
enabling access to all Availability Zones (AZs) within that region to host your applications.
You create subnets within specific AZs, allowing you to define subnetworks in the VPC when
deploying your applications. This setup lets you host replica workloads across multiple
subnets and AZs, enhancing high availability in case of an AZ outage.
Multiple VPCs within a region or across different regions can be connected using VPC Peering,
which enables routing traffic between VPCs over AWS's private network. This reduces costs
associated with internet traffic and enhances security. You can also host different components
of your applications across multiple VPCs—for example, compute services in one VPC with a
peering connection to another VPC hosting backend databases. This approach adds security
layers by restricting access to specific VPCs based on administrative and engineering needs. For
example, you might ensure that database administrators only have access to VPCs hosting
databases while restricting access to web servers.
For more complex network connectivity, AWS offers the VPC Transit Gateway, which
provides a hub-and-spoke model to connect multiple VPCs. This eliminates the need for
individual peering connections, reducing operational complexity.
You can also connect your VPCs to on-premises locations using VPNs or AWS Direct Connect.
The latter provides higher bandwidth and routes traffic over private networks, bypassing the
public internet entirely.
Ultimately, VPCs are designed to help you build secure, private networks in the cloud, isolating
workloads and ensuring that only authorized inbound and outbound traffic reaches your
applications.

At the core of every application lies a compute resource — the technology that powers
computational processing and data operations. Computing capacity has evolved significantly
over time. In the early days, this was provided by physical servers. A server is a computer or
software system that delivers resources, services, or data to other computers, known as clients,
over a network. However, physical servers had limited processing power, memory, and storage
capacity. Due to these constraints—and challenges related to application compatibility, such
as shared libraries and runtime environments—businesses typically dedicate a single physical
server to each application. As a result, organizations maintained large banks of servers to
support their various business applications, often requiring significant real estate, either on-
premises or in co-located data centers, to accommodate their extensive infrastructure.
With the advent of virtualization and an increase in compute resources such as CPU (Central
Processing Unit) capacity, memory, and storage, it was now possible to host multiple virtual
machines (virtual servers) on a single physical host machine. This means that you can now run
multiple applications on a single physical server, all isolated from each other within their own
virtual machines. This avoided compatibility issues while reducing the overall footprint of
physical hardware.
In this chapter, you will explore Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2). This service enables
you to deploy virtual machines, providing the compute capacity needed to run applications
ranging from simple websites to advanced artificial intelligence and data analytics workloads.
Additionally, you will learn about other AWS compute services, including containerization,
which offers a more efficient alternative to traditional virtual machines, and serverless
architectures powered by event-driven compute services, which significantly reduce
administrative overhead and provide a highly cost-effective solution.

Understanding Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is one of AWS's core service offerings,
allowing you to launch virtual servers in the idx_0ecb383d cloud. You can deploy servers running various
operating systems, including a wide range of Linux distributions (such as Ubuntu, Red Hat,
and Amazon Linux), Windows Server, and even macOS. Access to these virtual machines is
provided at the operating system level, enabling you to configure the guest OS to suit your
application's needs—install tools, manage patches, and perform upgrades.
Virtual machines run on virtualization software idx_c20d6cec known as a hypervisor. You may be familiar
with hypervisors in on-premises environments, such as VMware or Microsoft Hyper-V.
Amazon EC2 instances run on a customized version of the Nitro Hypervisor. This
customization minimizes overhead and offloads most virtualization tasks to dedicated
hardware, allowing EC2 instances to achieve near-bare-metal performance.
Hypervisor software allows you to partition physical hardware into virtualized representations
of physical components such as CPU, memory, and storage, presenting them as virtual
machines—each isolated from the others and functioning as a complete server. In an on-
premises environment, you can access the hypervisor layer to create virtual machines, select
virtual components, and configure them to meet your specific requirements. For example, you
might configure a virtual machine with two virtual CPU cores, 6GB of memory, and 1TB of root
volume capacity. Each virtual machine hosts its own guest operating system, applications, and
utilities as required, preventing conflicts due to compatibility issues.
With Amazon EC2, the underlying hypervisor is abstracted away from you. Instead, you access
a self-service portal (or use the CLI) and choose from various configuration options, including
CPU capacities, memory allocations, networking bandwidth, storage types, and operating
systems. These EC2 instances are categorized into instance families, types, and sizes for easy
selection and comparison.

AWS offers the Elastic Block Storage (EBS) solution, which functions similarly to attaching a
storage volume as a virtual hard disk idx_5f5dbabe from a Storage Area Network (SAN) in an idx_5591d140 on-premises
environment. You can create a volume with the desired capacity and attach it to a virtual
machine as either a root volume (which is made bootable and typically hosts the operating
system) or a data volume. Once connected, you format it with a file system that the operating
system recognizes.
AWS EBS volumes are categorized into Solid State Drives (SSDs) and Hard Disk Drives (HDDs).
SSDs are optimized for transactional idx_9c693e1d workloads that require frequent, low-latency read/write
operations (measured in IOPS). They are ideal for boot volumes, databases, and latency-
sensitive idx_530fd311 applications. However, HDDs are optimized for sequential throughput and are better
suited for large streaming workloads such as log processing and data warehousing.
The following SSD volume types are offered as part of EBS:
gp3: At the time of writing this chapter, gp3 idx_cd6647ca volumes are the latest generation of low-
cost SSD volumes offered by AWS. These volumes are ideal for most transactional
workloads, provide low latency, and are well-suited as boot volumes. Compared to the
previous generation (gp2), gp3 volumes are 20% more cost-effective and allow
independent scaling of volume performance regardless of volume size. They offer a
baseline performance of 3,000 IOPS, which can scale up to a maximum of 16,000 IOPS.
Regarding capacity, gp3 volumes can be provisioned between 1 GiB and 16 TiB. AWS
recommends migrating from gp2 to gp3 for better cost efficiency and performance.
io1: Provisioned IOPS SSDs (io1) offer higher performance and are designed for critical
I/O idx_0d8a494c intensive workloads such as databases, which are often sensitive to consistent
levels of performance and consistency. These volumes range from 4GiB to 64TiB, and
you can provision between 100 IOPS and 64,000 IOPS. Note that you can achieve up to
64,000 IOPS only on Nitro Systems, whereas on other systems, the maximum
performance is up to 32,000 IOPS.
io2 Block Express: Built on idx_64037399 the next generation of EC2 storage architecture, the io2
Block Express is designed for the most demanding I/O-intensive applications. It is ideal
for critical workloads such as Oracle databases, SAP HANA, Microsoft SQL Server, and
similar high-end applications. You get sub-millisecond average latency, and storage
capacity of up to 64TiB, performance of up to 256,000 IOPS, and volume throughput of
up to 4,000 MiB/s.

The following are some additional features of AWS Elastic Block Store (EBS) volumes:
EBS volumes idx_c0d55bc5 are connected over a storage network and can be attached to or detached
from an EC2 instance. If an instance experiences a failure, you can detach the EBS
volumes and attach them to another instance to continue accessing the data stored on
them.
You can take snapshots of your EBS volumes as part of your disaster recovery and
backup strategy. The first snapshot of a volume is always a full backup, while
subsequent snapshots are incremental, capturing only the changes made since the last
snapshot. These snapshots are stored in Amazon S3 and fully managed by AWS.
Additionally, snapshots can be copied across regions, allowing you to create new
volumes in different regions. They can also be shared with other AWS accounts.
EBS volumes are network-attached storage that provide persistent block-level storage
for EC2 instances. They exist independently of any instance's lifecycle.
In the next section, you will learn about another type of block storage—instance store volumes
—and understand their use case. These volumes are directly attached to the physical host on
which your EC2 instance is deployed.
AWS EC2 instance store volumes
AWS instance store volumes are local idx_158e5493 storage drives physically attached to the host where your
EC2 instance is deployed.
The primary benefit of instance store volumes is their ultra-high throughput and low latency,
making them ideal for workloads requiring fast, temporary storage. Another advantage is that

However, instance store volumes are not persistent. Data stored on them remains available
only while the instance is running on the same physical host as the volume. If you stop and
restart an EC2 instance, AWS may launch it on a different host, and all instance store volumes
will be lost. AWS recommends that instance store volumes be used only for temporary data.
While block storage is typically used to host the operating system and install applications on
EC2 instances, it is not ideal for sharing data and files between instances.
Often, you may have a central repository of data that needs to be accessible by multiple EC2
instances. While it is possible to configure file shares on an EBS-backed EC2 instance using NFS
(Network File System) or SMB (Server Message Block) protocols, this approach is cumbersome
and can experience performance issues, primarily if instances are distributed across different
Availability Zones in a region. This is because EBS volumes are availability zone-specific and
need to be attached to instances in idx_af6ed966 the AZ it is deployed in.
Instead, AWS offers dedicated file storage solutions designed specifically for shared access. The
following section introduces two such offerings:
Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) – A idx_bc34562d scalable, fully managed NFS file system for
Linux instances
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server – A fully managed file system that provides
SMB-based shared storage for idx_31dd25e6 Windows workloads
Let's look at them in more detail in the following subsections.
Amazon Elastic File System
Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) allows idx_60c2120a you to create a shared file system within a region
and configure mount points accessible across multiple Availability Zones. EC2 instances within
these Availability Zones can mount the EFS file system, providing a common directory
structure for shared file access.
Amazon EFS is designed for Linux-based EC2 instances and supports the NFS protocol for file
sharing. Once configured, you create a file system and set up mount targets in each Availability
Zone where instances need access.

Choosing EC2 pricing options
AWS idx_8b0757f1 offers a variety of pay-as-you-go pricing options for its EC2 service. You don't need to
make a significant upfront investment in physical servers. Instead, based on your business
requirements, you only pay for the hours your compute resources are in use. If you stop an
instance but keep it in your account, you won't incur compute charges while it remains in a
stopped state. This pricing model is the On-Demand pricing option and is the default method
for procuring compute capacity on AWS. The following pricing options are available:
On-demand pricing options
The on-demand pricing option idx_a3869c13 is the default idx_73d0992b pricing model for launching EC2 instances. You
are charged an hourly rate, billed per second (with a minimum charge of 60 seconds), for the
duration your instance remains in the running state. This charge includes all bundled
operating system licensing costs unless you choose to bring your own enterprise licensing
agreement. It also covers any bundled applications that come with the instance.
The on-demand pricing model is ideal for customers who require the flexibility to consume
compute resources on a pay-as-you-go basis. Customers can deploy instances in their AWS
account and are only billed for compute costs while the instances run—this pricing option best
suits short-term, spiky, or unpredictable workloads. For example, suppose you need to deploy
a set of test servers to run application test cases for a few weeks before rolling out a production
application. In that case, On-Demand pricing offers a cost-effective solution. Since these

Reserved instance pricing option
This pricing model idx_0a5837fc offers significant cost idx_46cc72cf savings—up to 72% off the On-Demand price—for
customers who commit to a 1-year or 3-year agreement for a specific compute capacity.
Designed to encourage long-term commitments, Reserved Instance pricing is ideal for
workloads that require continuous operation 24/7 throughout the year, such as corporate
websites, e-commerce platforms, and global customer-facing applications.
It is important to note that Reserved Instances are not actual EC2 instances that you provision.
Instead, they represent a pricing agreement that grants the customer the right to run a specific
EC2 instance configuration in a designated AWS region for a fixed term (1 year or 3 years) at a
discounted rate. Once you launch an instance matching the reserved configuration within the
specified region (or an Availability Zone, depending on the Reserved Instance type), the
Reserved Instance pricing is idx_97754777 applied automatically instead of the standard On-Demand rate.
There are two Reserved Instance pricing options:
Standard Reserved Instance: This idx_7214c108 option provides the highest discount—up to 72%—
depending on the length of the commitment and whether you make an all-upfront
payment (discussed later). While Standard Reserved Instances offer significant cost
savings, they come with limited idx_4796eb87 flexibility. You can modify certain attributes, such as:
The Availability Zone within the same region
The instance size (within the same instance family)
The network type
The on-demand pricing option only applies to the cost of computing capacity. It does
not include the cost of any attached block storage volumes. For block storage, you are
charged based on the total amount of provisioned storage, even if the instances are in a
stopped state.
